implementation_notes: java.lang.reflect.Proxy.newProxyInstance creates the proxy class at run time for the interface list you pass and routes every invocation - including equals/hashCode/toString - to one InvocationHandler.invoke that receives the proxy, the reflected Method and the boxed arguments; since Java 16 the handler can invoke an interface default method through InvocationHandler.invokeDefault. It requires interfaces, and proxy classes for the same interface permutation are reused, so generation happens once per loader. The classic structure stays justified exactly when the interface set is only known at run time; otherwise a hand-written decorator is clearer and faster.
pitfalls: Interfaces only: proxying a class needs bytecode generation, and final classes plus final or private methods stay unproxyable even then.
method.invoke wraps the target's exception in InvocationTargetException, and a checked exception outside the interface's throws clause surfaces as UndeclaredThrowableException.
Calls the target makes on itself (this.bar()) never pass the proxy, and generated classes together with handlers are a classloader-leak vector in long-lived containers.
The proxy is not an instance of the target class, so getClass(), fields and casts to the implementation see the proxy rather than the real object.

variants.name: runtime subclass proxy via bytecode generation
variants.idiom_name: Byte Buddy (or CGLIB) subclass proxy with MethodDelegation interceptors
variants.implementation_notes: When the target has no interface, a library generates a subclass at run time: Spring AOP falls back to CGLIB, and Byte Buddy is the modern replacement - subclass(Target.class).method(matcher).intercept(MethodDelegation.to(Interceptor.class)) overrides non-final methods and reloads the class through MethodHandles.Lookup so the Java module system stays happy. The proxy is an instance of the target class, so it can be injected wherever the class is expected, but final classes, final/private methods and non-visible package-private members remain unproxyable.
pitfalls: Constructor bypassing (Objenesis, sun.misc.Unsafe) skips field initialisation and breaks across JDK upgrades; prefer strategies that call a real super constructor.
Class loading strategies matter: a fresh child loader per proxy leaks and breaks identity, while injection into an existing loader needs MethodHandles.Lookup or opened packages.
Final classes cannot be subclassed and final or private methods cannot be advised, so 'proxy everything' designs fail on exactly the types that need interception most.

variants.name: annotation-processor generated proxy
variants.idiom_name: annotation processor emitting the forwarding class at build time
variants.implementation_notes: An annotation processor (or a build plugin) can emit the forwarding class at compile time for a declared interface, which removes runtime code generation and reflection entirely - the version that works under GraalVM native image, with JPMS encapsulation, and in security-reviewed builds. It costs a build step, one generated class per opted-in interface, and a mechanism for the caller to select the generated proxy, so it is chosen for AOT and auditability rather than for flexibility.
pitfalls: Generated classes must be regenerated in every build (IDE, CI, release); a stale artifact keeps forwarding the old interface and the failure appears as an AbstractMethodError.
The generated proxy must be wired explicitly (factory, DI binding), so the 'invisible' interception of a runtime proxy is replaced by code that must be kept in the wiring.
